title: An Information-Theoretic Framework For Optimizing Experimental Design To Distinguish Probabilistic Neural Codes
claim: Two rival hypotheses differ in where prior knowledge enters: after sensory encoding (likelihood) or already within early sensory responses (posterior).
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left-to-right flow, brain schematic with color-coded distributions
description: Two side-by-side panels, A) Likelihood Coding Hypothesis and B) Posterior Coding Hypothesis, each showing a brain silhouette in side view. In each panel a world-state orientation symbol feeds a grating stimulus via green arrows into visual cortex (V1). A magnified circle shows spike rasters for the V1 population. Small Gaussian plots labeled Prior (blue), Likelihood Function (green) and Posterior (magenta) sit over the brain. In A, V1 is green and encodes the likelihood. A blue prior feed from a higher area combines with it downstream into a magenta posterior, which leads to a black Decision/Behavior arrow. In B, V1 is magenta and encodes the posterior directly, because the blue prior feeds back into V1. A magenta arrow then leads to Decision/Behavior. The eye goes first to the bold titles and the green versus magenta V1 coloring.
caption: Two competing hypotheses on how sensory uncertainty information is encoded in early sensory neural populations. A) Likelihood coding hypothesis, exemplified by the probabilistic population code [ref], proposes that early sensory populations encode the likelihood function over the stimulus, with posterior computation deferred to downstream areas. B) Posterior coding hypothesis, exemplified by the neural sampling code [ref], posits that early sensory populations readily encode the posterior distribution over hidden world state by integrating prior knowledge conveyed via feedback connections from higher cortical areas.
abstract: The Bayesian brain hypothesis has been a leading theory in understanding perceptual decision-making under uncertainty. While extensive psychophysical evidence supports the notion of the brain performing Bayesian computations, how uncertainty information is encoded in sensory neural populations remains elusive. Specifically, two competing hypotheses propose that early sensory populations encode either the likelihood function (exemplified by probabilistic population codes) or the posterior distribution (exemplified by neural sampling codes) over the stimulus, with the key distinction lying in whether stimulus priors would modulate the neural responses. However, experimentally differentiating these two hypotheses has remained challenging, as it is unclear what task design would effectively distinguish the two. In this work, we present an information-theoretic framework for optimizing the task stimulus distribution that would maximally differentiate competing probabilistic neural codes. To quantify how distinguishable the two probabilistic coding hypotheses are under a given task design, we derive the information gap--the expected performance difference when likelihood versus posterior decoders are applied to neural populations--by evaluating the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true posterior and a task-marginalized surrogate posterior. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that the information gap accurately predicts decoder performance differences across diverse task settings. Critically, maximizing the information gap yields stimulus distributions that optimally differentiate likelihood and posterior coding hypotheses. Our framework enables principled, theory-driven experimental designs with maximal discriminative power to differentiate probabilistic neural codes, advancing our understanding of how neural populations represent and process sensory uncertainty.
